# Enhancing teacher AI literacy and integration through different types of cases in teacher professional development 

## Ai-Chu Elisha Ding [a,\*, Lehong Shi](#computers-and-education-open) [a, Haotian Yang](#computers-and-education-open) [a, Ikseon Choi](#computers-and-education-open) [b ](#computers-and-education-open)

a _Department of Workforce Education and Instructional Technology, University of Georgia, 131 River’s Crossing 850, College Station Road, Athens, GA 30602, United States_ 

b _Nell Hodgson Woodruff School of Nursing, Emory University, United States_ 

ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT 

_Keywords:_ Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into teaching practices is increasingly vital for preparing students for a AI integration technology-centric future. This study examined the influence of a case-based AI professional development (PD) Teacher professional development program on AI integration strategies and AI literacy among seven middle school science teachers. Employing Case problems 

three distinct case problems, from well-structured to ill-structured, the AI PD program aimed to stimulate 

Cased-based discussion Teacher AI literacy teachers’ reflection on AI literacy development and encourage the construction of problem-solving and AI 

integration strategies within various pedagogical contexts. Analysis of video-recorded case discussions revealed that teachers primarily drew on personal experiences for collaborative problem-solving across the three cases. However, the complexity of the case problems influenced their approach to knowledge co-construction, and dealing with ill-structured problems promoted the application of new knowledge. Through analyzing the survey data, we found a marked increase in teachers’ AI literacy, particularly in the domain of knowing and under- standing AI, suggesting a pivotal role for direct instruction that supports AI literacy growth. However, their application of this AI knowledge was limited during the case discussions, while other domains of teacher AI literacy were more frequently employed. The findings highlight the importance of combining direct instruction with case-based discussions in AI-related PD programs to bolster teacher AI literacy effectively. The research has implications for using a case-based learning approach during short-term PD initiatives and advocates the ongoing need for comprehensive AI literacy development to facilitate teachers’ AI integration in subject-specific teaching.

and their replication of the AI curriculum in their future teaching (e.g., \[[14,15\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in)). 

To address this PD need, we focus on designing and providing a meaningful and content-specific teacher AI PD that enhances teachers’ fundamental understanding of AI literacy as well as AI integration practices. We intentionally designed our PD based on the case-based learning (CBL) method \[[16,17\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) as it situates complex learning tasks in authentic scenarios, allowing teachers to apply their knowledge and skills to real-world situations. However, there have been no reports of AI-related PD utilizing CBL to date. We also lack insights about how different types of AI integration cases can influence teachers’ learning experiences and engagement and how teachers will develop and employ their AI literacy during CBL. Thus, in this study, we answered the following two research questions: 

1. In what ways did different types of AI integration cases elicit different teacher learning experiences? 
2. How did teachers’ self-reported AI literacy change following the case-based AI professional development program? 

2\. **Theoretical framework** 

_2.1._ _Teachers’ artificial intelligence integration_ 

In recent years, the increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into various sectors of society has been a subject of significant in- terest and development, with education being one of the areas most impacted. AI educational tools such as intelligent tutoring systems \[[4\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) and automatic scoring and feedback systems \[[18,19\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) have the potential to help teachers offer adaptive materials and activities for personalized learning experiences as well as timely and customized feedback for all students \[[20,21\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). Furthermore, AI-enabled teaching assistants \[[22,23\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) can assist teachers with various instructional tasks, such as responding to inquiries, grading assignments, and interacting with students. Despite the potential of AI to transform teaching, the critical of the matter lies in fostering teachers’ meaningful integration of various AI applications into real-world classroom settings. Teachers’ meaningful AI integration in content area teaching would refer to how they leverage the diverse capabilities of AI to augment learning and teaching in pedagogically and ethically sound ways, differentiating from teaching AI knowledge and concepts to students, which is the focus of many studies (e.g., \[[24–26\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in)). The literature on teacher technology integration has emphasized that one critical key to the successful adoption and integration of emerging technology is teachers’ knowledge about the pedagogically sound strategies, coupled with their skills and compe- tencies to effectively integrate varied technology tools into their peda- gogical practices \[[27,6,28\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). Specifically, in the realm of AI integration in education, this necessitates not just a technical familiarity with AI ap- plications’ functions and operations but also a nuanced understanding of how these different AI applications can be leveraged to support and enhance teaching in a pedagogically effective and appropriate manner \[[29,5,14\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). Therefore, equipping teachers with strategies and skills that are pedagogically sound is essential for their adept and impactful inte- gration of AI in complex educational situations. 

_2.2._ _The four domains of teacher AI literacy_ 

Teachers’ integration of advanced AI technologies to renovate educational practices requires proficiency in AI literacy. Long and Magerko \[[30\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) defined AI literacy as “a set of competencies that enables individuals to evaluate AI technologies critically; communicate and collaborate effectively with AI; and use AI as a tool online, at home, and in the workplace” (p. 598). Within educational contexts, teachers’ AI literacy can be characterized by the requisite knowledge and skills, the methods for collaboratively engaging with AI, and the capacity to assess the pedagogical and ethical implications of their AI integration 

endeavors in teaching and learning. Enhancing teachers’ AI literacy could mitigate issues arising from their limited understanding of and experience with AI tools in instruction, thus promoting teachers’ com- petencies to adopt AI in teaching \[[9,10\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). Moreover, enhanced AI literacy enables teachers to effectively employ appropriate pedagogical strate- gies and contemplate ethical considerations, excelling in the rapidly evolving AI-augmented educational landscape \[[11,31\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). 

To frame AI literacy in educational contexts, Ng et al. \[[32\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) proposed a four-dimensional framework consisting of knowing and understanding AI, applying AI applications, creating and evaluating AI applications, and considering ethical issues. Zhao et al. \[[33\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) employed this framework to investigate teachers’ AI literacy. First, _Knowing and Understanding AI_ is foundational, as it is imperative for teachers to comprehend funda- mental AI concepts with enhanced AI familiarity \[[11\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). Second, _Applying AI applications_ is critical as teachers move beyond conceptual knowledge about AI to utilizing it in teaching practices and leveraging its potential to enhance teaching and learning experiences. Zhao et al. \[[33\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) found that this domain is dominant among the four domains of teacher AI literacy. Third, _evaluating AI applications_ for their pedagogical utility, efficacy, and appropriateness becomes increasingly crucial as AI’s role in pedagogy continues to evolve \[[11,34\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). It is critical for teachers to employ a critical lens to examine the potential and limitations of AI implementation. Lastly, reflecting on _AI ethics_ involves teachers’ contemplation of how to align AI integration in teaching with ethical standards and educational values by taking into consideration issues such as AI bias, student privacy, equity and fairness, and the broader ramifications of AI technologies for society \[[35,36\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). Fig. 1 presents the four domains of teacher AI literacy discussed by Zhao et al. \[[33\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). 

_2.3._ _Case-based AI professional development and the design of case problems_ 

Case-based learning (CBL) involves using real-world scenarios to stimulate discussion, analysis, and problem-solving \[[16\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). It is ideal for an AI teacher PD program as it supports teachers’ consideration of the interplay among pedagogy, content, and AI technology within real-world teaching contexts. 

CBL learning experience typically involves problem-finding and problem-solving space. Jonassen \[[17\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) defines problem-finding as the first step in the problem-solving process, which is identifying and articulating an unknown entity in a focal situation, for which a clear and concise problem description is crucial. Solution-finding involves generating and evaluating potential solutions \[[37\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in), requiring a deep understanding of the problem context and the ability to conduct activity-based manipulation within the problem space. 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 1.** The four domains of teacher AI literacy. 

Research indicates that in the processes of problem-finding and problem-solving, individuals heavily depend on personal experiences as their main source of knowledge, utilizing these experiences as a basis for interpreting situations and formulating solutions \[[38\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). This reliance on personal experience underscores the inherent nature of CBL, where real-world scenarios facilitate contextual learning \[[39\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). However, as highlighted by Shulman \[[40\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in), the design and facilitation of case dis- cussions are pivotal in encouraging participants to not only tap into their existing knowledge pools but also to assimilate new information and skills. This involves crafting case problems and discussions that prompt participants to engage with diverse sources of information, such as well-structured and ill-structured problems \[[17\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in), thereby fostering a comprehensive understanding and application of concepts. That said, the design of the problems in a case plays a critical role in fostering meaningful case-based discussion. Shulman and Colbert \[[41\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) emphasize that case problems should be catalysts for discussion, fostering collaborative exploration of various educational issues. Jon- assen and Hung \[[42\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) underscore the importance of structuring case problems and posit that well-designed case problems should be authentic, representing real-world complexities and encouraging active exploration and reflection. In CBL, well-designed case problems could have a significant impact on the problem solver’s perspective on and experience with the problem, including confidence, ability to use prior learning, and attitude \[[42\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). Jonassen \[[17\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) categorizes problems into several types along a continuum based on their level of structure, ranging from well-structured, moderately-structured, and ill-structured (see Fig. 2). Furthermore, Choi and Lee \[[43\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) emphasized the impor- tance of utilizing ill-structured problems in CBL, highlighting its role in enabling learners to develop skills essential for addressing complex and dynamic real-world situations. Drawing on the problem typology in Jonassen \[[17\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in), we meticulously chose three distinct types of problems for designing the AI PD case studies: rule-using induction problems (well-structured), diagnosis-solution problems (moderately-structured), and dilemmas (ill-structured). Fig. 2 shows the position of the three types of problems on the continuum from well-structured to ill-structured. 

Rule-using induction problems, representing the well-structured type in Jonassen’s \[[17\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) problem typology, are characterized by applying established rules or procedures to new situations. These problems have clearly defined objectives and can be employed when learners are introduced to unfamiliar devices or systems \[[44\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). For instance, Mitchell et al. \[[45\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) highlighted the importance of well-structured PD problems for promoting teachers’ integration of diverse content and pedagogical expertise to develop technology-enhanced, inquiry-based lessons. 

Diagnosis-solution problems are critical intermediaries between well-structured rule-using induction problems and complex dilemmas. Such problems require learners to identify and analyze specific issues based on given symptoms or indicators and then derive solutions based on their deductions \[[17\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). This process allows for the utilization of multiple paths to analyze the source of the anomaly driving the problem and determine various diagnostic possibilities, a practice that cultivates learners’ analytical skills and creativity \[[42\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). Moreover, when learners engage in group-based, collaborative problem-solving, they can become active constructors of knowledge, leading to improved academic 

**Fig. 2.**

performance [\[46\].](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) 

Dilemmas, representing the most ill-structured problems, are char-

acterized by their inherent complexity and lack of clear resolution, often involving scenarios that involve navigating through a spectrum of ethical, moral, and practical considerations to reach the most feasible rather than the ideal solution \[[44\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). Rahmawati et al. \[[47\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) argue that the ill-structured nature of dilemmas effectively challenges learners to develop critical thinking, creativity, and argumentation skills. The fea- tures of dilemmas are precious for developing teachers’ ethical reasoning and decision-making skills in integrating emerging and transformative technologies. 

Currently, it is less known how types of problems would impact 

teachers’ uses of sources of knowledge co-construction during case- based discussions, thereby influencing their learning experiences and AI literacy. By incorporating three types of cases and exploring how teachers learned through the various AI integration cases, the current study will be able to provide preliminary insights into the design of cases for teacher AI PD. 

3\. **Methods** 

_3.1._ _Research context_ 

The current study is part of a two-phased project, reporting findings 

from the second phase of an ongoing investigation of ways to advance K- 12 teachers’ AI literacy and enhance their integration of AI technologies into classroom practices. The initial phase involved observing and examining middle school science teachers’ initial experience of incor- porating an AI-powered educational tool called Inquiry Intelligent Tutoring System (Inq-ITS) into their science classrooms for one semester \[[7\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). 

Building on the objectives of our project to promote consistent and 

skilled use of AI by teachers and the reported teaching challenges identified through our Phase 1 study, the current phase (the study) was designed to offer this group of teachers a well-designed AI professional development program. This research investigated how teachers construct strategies for AI integration within diverse pedagogical con- texts through participation in case discussions. We also aimed to assess the AI literacy teachers demonstrated and employed in constructing various AI integration strategies and solutions. 

_3.2._ _Participants_ 

The participants were seven science teachers from the focal middle 

school who participated in a case-based PD program focused on enhancing their AI integration into teaching. They were randomly divided into two groups for case-based discussions. Each teacher had access to various PD materials, including handouts, Google Slides, and the dedicated AI PD website. Additionally, they could interact with online pre- and post-surveys using their personal laptops or mobile devices. 

Table 1 displays teachers’ demographic backgrounds and previous 

experiences using AI in classrooms. Four of the teachers had experienced integrating the Inquiry Intelligent Tutoring System (Inq-ITS) into their instructional practices before the AI PD. In contrast, the other three

_3.3._ _Case-based AI professional development program_ 

In the summer of 2023, we developed and delivered a 4 h AI PD to engage science teachers to discuss the best AI integration strategies and enhance their AI literacy. The AI PD was structured around a case-based learning approach, featuring three distinct case problems for hands-on and collaborative learning experiences. All teachers participated in the AI PD in person and have access to PD materials and survey questions from personal computers or mobile devices. 

The PD session focused on introducing the following topics: (1) Defining and introducing AI and AI literacy, (2) Leveraging AI tools and instructional strategies to support multilingual learners in science classrooms, (3) Best practices for the implementation of Inq-ITS, and (4) Responsible use of AI. Table 2 provides a detailed summary of the AI PD topics and corresponding activities during each topic. 

The PD session began with an instructor-led lecture to establish a shared foundation of AI technology beginning with an explanation of what generative AI is and how techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, and neural networks are used to generate new informa- tion. We also reviewed the “Five Big Ideas in AI” presented by the AI4k12 initiative ([https://ai4k12.org)](https://ai4k12.org), providing concise examples relevant to science education. Fig. 3 illustrates the first big idea of AI: perception and corresponding examples. In addition, we delved into the definition and significance of AI literacy for teachers. Beyond the con- ceptual knowledge of AI, we demonstrated practical AI applications, such as ChatGPT and Stable Diffusion, offering teachers hands-on interaction with AI. 

The core of the AI PD session was three case problem scenarios, each crafted in alignment with the problem typology in Jonassen \[[17\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in); details are explained in Section 2.3. The first case, “¡no entiendo!”, following the principles of the rule-using induction problem type, was designed to prompt teachers to reflect critically on how to address multilingual learners’ needs in classrooms to enhance their learning utilizing the strategies and AI tools introduced during the lecture. In this case, we clearly defined the teacher’s struggles and failures in instructing multilingual learners effectively and provided a set of driving questions to prompt teachers’ discussion of the case problems and solutions (see Fig. 4 for a snapshot of the case). Participants were prompted to pick one instructional problem in the case to focus on: Discuss what strategies, activities, or tools you recommend to Miss Lexi for solving the problem. adept use of AI educational products in daily teaching, increased by 1.143 points, and item 1, assessing teachers’ identification of AI tech- nology in educational AI products or services, increased by 1.142 points. To be noted, the first domain of _Knowing and Understanding AI_, including items 1 and 2, witnessed the most significant average increase of approximately 1.1 points. This increase demonstrated the notable progress in teachers’ fundamental understanding of AI technology, knowledge, and concepts attributable to the AI PD program. However, as highlighted in the results addressing Research Question 1, teachers drew little upon this AI literacy domain when identifying instructional problems and co-constructing solutions during the three case-based discussions. 

Qualitative analysis of the pre-and post-survey open-ended questions further demonstrated the shifts in teachers’ AI literacy. Before the AI PD, teachers expressed a limited grasp of AI literacy, only two out of the seven teachers reporting rudimentary AI knowledge and AI integration and the rest having had no prior exposure to AI technology in teaching. This picture was transformed dramatically in the post-survey phase, in which six of the seven teachers reported a heightened sense of AI literacy and showed marked confidence in integrating AI in pedagogical prac- tices and enthuisastic anticipation of the multitude of instructional op- portunities for AI integration. 

In the _Knowledge and Understanding AI_ domain, teachers exhibited a broadened scope of AI knowledge following the AI PD, which had expanded to encompass foundational AI concepts and applications, such as machine learning, the various levels of AI, and various AI tools. They were particularly alert to the implications of generative AI and concerns related to academic dishonesty. This expansion of AI knowledge was accompanied by an increase in favorable attitudes towards using AI in educational contexts, in contrast with the initial mixed feelings expressed by most teachers. 

Regarding the _Applying AI Applications_ domain, a significant shift was noted in teachers’ preparedness to employ AI in future instructional activities. After the AI PD, they displayed an eagerness to experiment with various AI tools introduced during the AI PD, such as ChatGPT, Stable Diffusion, and automatic translators, into their teaching for pur- poses such as adjusting reading difficulty levels, assisting students in gathering information and organizing ideas, and providing personalized feedback. 

In the _Evaluation of AI Applicatio_ns domain, teachers initially concentrated on the implications of AI for teachers. After the training, their focus broadened to include ethical considerations, such as stu- dents’ direct use of AI-generated content. They also emphasized estab- lishing guidelines for evaluating AI applications in classrooms. Lastly, concerning the domain of _AI Ethics_, a change in teachers’ awareness of potential issues was discernible. Initially concerned with issues like data privacy and plagiarism, teachers now intend to employ tools for monitoring plagiarism and assessing the appropriateness of AI use. They further indicated plans and strategies to integrate ethical guidelines for and expectations of AI use into classroom policies and engage students in conversations about AI’s ethical and responsible use. 

5. **Discussion** 

This study explored using a case-based learning approach to support science teachers’ co-construction of solutions and strategies for solving instructional problems involving AI integration. We presented three types of case problems on a spectrum ranging from well-structured to moderately-structured to ill-structured, represented by a rule-based in- duction problem, a diagnosis-solution problem, and a dilemma, respectively \[[17,42\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) (see Fig. 2). By shedding light on how teachers explicated AI integration during case discussions, this study also offers initial insights into how the leveling structuring of instructional design case problems may impact teachers’ learning of AI integration and the development of AI literacy. 

First, our findings suggest that during case-based discussions, the 

participating teachers are oriented to critically examine AI tools’ pedagogical affordances and technical design and identify potential learning struggles as problem-finding. They also drew on their personal experiences and practical knowledge when placing critical instructional issues \[55\]. In doing so, they were able to consider the pedagogical use of a novel technology in terms of learners’ characteristics. Additionally, our findings show that, having been only recently introduced to AI literacy, the teachers relied heavily on their previous experiences to generate solutions for solving identified problems in all three cases. This approach to solution construction is consistent with findings from Palmer and Choi \[56\], who suggest that individuals rely largely on their prior experiences to reason about new problems. More importantly, humans tend to solve a new problem by considering a similar past problem and adapting its solution to the latest problem \[57\]. Thus, it is unsurprising that the teachers used retrieving personal experience as their primary approach to solution construction during case-based discussions, even when topics such as AI represented unfa- miliar territory. In their case-based reasoning, the participants identified the similarities between the current problem and past problems they had experienced, retrieved the solutions to the most similar past problems, and adapted these to fit the current problem \[56\]. This finding confirms that personal experience should be an essential resource for problem-finding and problem-solving in case-based discussions. While the participants used prior experience as their major source of solution construction, their solution construction patterns varied among the different types of cases. Our analysis shows that a problem’s level of structure played a crucial role in determining the strategies the partic- ipants used to solve it. We found that the moderately- and ill-structured problems provided more scope for participants to apply and generate new knowledge beyond their existing knowledge and experiences. For example, the teachers spent more time discussing the solutions and developing new ideas (_n_ = 16) for the second case, which presented a diagnosis-solution problem \[[17,42\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) than for the first case, which showed a rule-using problem (_n_ = 2). In the third case, which presented a dilemma, teachers used pedagogical knowledge introduced in the PD and generated new ideas (_n_ = 22) more frequently than they consulted past personal experience for a solution (_n_ = 16). These findings align with the literature emphasizing the importance of using ill-structured problems for in-depth, collaborative, and meaningful inquiry-based learning \[55,58\]. Everyday teaching tasks are also complex, multi-faceted, and ill-structured \[[43,](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in)59\]. Therefore, we also recommend that teachers should engage in solving moderately- and ill-structured problems in AI professional development, especially in light of our findings showing that the moderately and ill-structured cases engen- dered more AI-related problem-finding and problem-solving discussions among the teachers. However, this does not mean well-structured problems, such as rule-using problems, are without value, which we will discuss further below. 

In terms of their AI literacy development, the participants reported growth in all four domains of AI literacy after completing our AI PD program. Interestingly, teachers perceived they had grown more in the AI knowledge domain (pre- and post-survey mean differ- ences=1.142–1.285) than in the other three domains, in which the mean differences ranged from 0.875 to 1.143. Yet, our video analysis revealed that the AI knowledge domain was rarely addressed in the case-based discussions (_n_ = 4), suggesting that the growth in AI knowledge was due mainly to the lectures given as part of the PD. However, this finding does not necessarily mean that the didactic lecture approach would be more effective than the case-based discussion activities for fostering teachers’ AI literacy. First, in their rankings of activities in the post-PD survey, our teachers preferred case-based discussions over lectures, and five of the seven teachers ranked case-based discussions as their most liked activities. Furthermore, as shown in the pre-survey data, only one teacher claimed basic knowledge about AI, while the remaining six reported scant AI knowledge and related experiences. Consequently, given the teachers’ low beginning competence in this domain, they 

could easily have perceived experiencing the most growth in the area. Our study has also shown that direction instruction still plays an essential role in case-based AI PD. As indicated by Table 2, we started our PD with a lecture to introduce teachers to the fundamental knowl- edge of AI, and the rule-using case was designed accordingly to engage teachers in applying the fundamental knowledge to solving the teaching problems. For the diagnosis-solution case, we provided direct instruc- tion on the procedural and technical knowledge of using a specific AI pedagogical tool (i.e., Inq-ITS) and then engaged teachers in noticing and solving problems related to the pedagogical and technical sides of integrating the tool. Finally, for the dilemma case, we chose to engage teachers in discussing the case first. Then, we proceeded with a whole- class discussion to synthesize what people have shared as the AI ethics problems and solutions in teaching and learning. The instructor then further offered a brief direction instruction on the various AI ethics concerns and potential instructional strategies. While the study mainly focused on teachers’ case-based discussions, as discussed above, the direction instructions still provided valuable insights about AI for teachers. To that end, it is important to balance direct instruction and case-based discussions and design ways to complement each other within the context of AI teacher PD. This leads to our insights into the missing design component in our AI case-based professional development. 

In hindsight, we realized that when developing the cases, especially the rule-using case, we assumed that, given their limited understanding of AI, teachers would rely on the AI knowledge and tools introduced in the lecture to construct instructional solutions for the case problems. However, when designing the cases and the discussion prompts for AI integration discussion, we failed to consider that in-service teachers might already have solutions to similar problems that they had encountered in the past without using AI tools, which would be natural for them to rely on instead of the newly encountered AI-based strategies introduced during the PD lecture. Furthermore, given that they were relatively unfamiliar with the new topic of AI knowledge and integra- tion, the teachers did not have a well-developed AI-related “case library” \[57\] to refer to when solving the instructional problems presented in the cases. As Mishra et al. \[[27\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) pointed out, to use AI tools in education, teachers must not only process knowledge about the technology but also integrate it with their prior pedagogical and content knowledge. That said, to apply the case-based learning approach to fostering teachers’ AI integration and AI literacy, a lecture before the case discussion would be necessary, but it is still not enough. Between the lecture and case-based discussion, in which teachers are prompted to develop instructional solutions, we recommend introducing additional _model cases_ in which the problems and solutions are presented \[60\]. We further recommend presenting well-structured problems, such as rule-using problems, in the model cases to help teachers see how new theories and tools can be applied in contexts. The additional model cases would help teachers bridge the gap between theory and practice and produce AI-integrated instructional solutions in case-based discussions with ill-structured problems. 

Finally, given the overall success of the case-based PD approach explored in this study, we recommend using case-based learning for short-term AI PD programs like ours. However, we acknowledge that sustainability is a concern for short-term AI PD and that we cannot claim the long-term effects of our PD. We agree with Yau et al. \[[26\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in) that AI education and AI literacy cover a vast range of knowledge and topics and a short-term program would not be able to cover a broad range of AI knowledge. It would be essetial that we also develop extended PD pro- grams to support subject area teachers’ AI literacy development and the integration of AI into subject area curricula. Yau et al. \[[26\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in), with the focus of integrating AI education in K-12 education, conceptualized through their PD experience that the initial teacher PD could focus on AI knowledge and pedgogy enhancement whereas the advanced PD con- cerns integrating AI education into different subject areas. Then, depending on in-service teachers’ technical and pedagogical 

background, they would go through different learning paths in the PD. Aligning with Yau et al’s recommendations, we also suggest starting with short-term introductory PD programs with case-based learning approach to introduce the basics of AI literacy, help teachers realize the potential and limitations of AI tools and stimulate their desire to in- crease their AI literacy and AI integration competence. Then, to support the integration of AI education across subject areas, extended AI teacher PD with different learning paths should be provided according to teachers’ technical backnground, subject areas, and years of experience with AI education \[[26\]](#education-23-wang-q-saha-k-gregori-e-joyner-d-goel-a-towards-mutual-theory-of-mind-in). 

6. **Conclusions** 

In sum, the present study provides insights into how the degree of structure of the instructional case problems may impact teachers’ con- struction of problem solutions and the development of AI literacy. For the design of short-term AI PD to initiate subject area teachers’ devel- opment of AI literacy and integration competence, we recommend the PD design using a lecture, a model case with well- and moderately- structured problems followed by case-based discussions of ill- structured problems. 

While this study contributes significantly to knowledge about teachers’ AI literacy development and AI integration practices in AI PD programs, it has limitations. First, the study involved a small number of participants, given the nature of the qualitative research, which focused on in-depth analysis and rich data collection from a specific group of middle school science teachers. This approach allowed for a concen- trated and manageable participant pool, facilitating detailed case-based discussions and personalized PD experiences. However, this limitation in participant size, while offering valuable insights into the development of AI literacy within this specific cohort, presents challenges to the generalizability of the findings. Future studies could benefit from a larger participant pool across diverse educational settings, including a broader range of subject areas and grade levels. This expansion would validate our findings and offer a more comprehensive view of AI inte- gration practices across the educational spectrum. Second, after the AI PD, there was no subsequent observation of teachers’ AI integration practices. While our confidence in the transferability of the PD-acquired AI literacy and integration strategies to actual classroom practices is cautiously optimistic, we recognize the need for empirical validation. The theoretical framework and pedagogical approaches employed in the PD program are grounded in established educational theories and practices, laying a solid foundation for effective AI integration. How- ever, without direct observation and follow-up, we could not confirm the degree to which participating teachers have applied the knowledge gained from the PD in their classroom practices. This gap underscores the importance of future research incorporating observational studies to empirically assess the application and impact of AI literacy in classroom settings. Future research should incorporate longitudinal designs that include follow-up observations and interviews with participating teachers. This approach would enable researchers to assess the sus- tainability and transferability of AI literacy and integration strategies from the PD to classroom practices. 

We encourage continued research into AI literacy, including devel- oping teaching cases that foster critical engagement in integrating AI across various subject areas. In that regard, more future research on teachers’ AI integration cases in different subject areas is vital to provide practical and subject-specific PD for supporting K-12 teachers’ AI inte- gration and AI literacy development. As highlighted in the study, pro- moting teachers’ AI literacy is vital for their effective and responsible implementation of AI in educational settings. The inevitable spread of technology in education necessitates equipping teachers with essential AI knowledge and enabling them to synergize this knowledge with their pedagogical expertise to develop AI-integrated and AI-focused curricula. In conclusion, enhancing teachers’ AI literacy and practical application is crucial to bolster their readiness to adopt emerging AI technologies in
